newsitem.title: INDIA: India sees no change in ties after Bhutto's fall.
newsitem.headline: India sees no change in ties after Bhutto's fall.

text.p: India reserved formal comment on Tuesday on Pakistani Prime Minister Benazir Bhutto's dismissal but officials said the move appeared to be backed by an army that opposed a militarist approach towards New Delhi.
"Basically, the situation will not affect us in any important way," an interior ministry official told Reuters.
"If the government has been dismissed to check instability, and if fresh elections are held soon, we have no worries," the official said.
A defence official in New Delhi said: "Our perception is that the current army leadership in Pakistan does not favour military adventurism against India.
"If our assessment is correct, the Pakistani government would not have been dismissed without the army's blessing," the official said.
There was no immediate high-level official reaction to Bhutto's sacking by presidential order.
An Indian foreign ministry official said they were waiting to hear from Foreign Minister Inder Gujral, now in Zimbabwe.
Gujral had accompanied Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda to Harare for a G-15 economic meeting of developing countries.
Carved out of British India in 1947 in a blood-stained partition of the subcontinent, neighbouring India and Pakistan have fought three wars, two of them over troubled Kashmir.
Pakistani President Farooq Leghari dismissed Bhutto's government early on Tuesday accusing it of corruption and misrule.

Former Indian foreign secretary Jyotindra Nath Dixit, the last Indian official to hold formal talks with Pakistan more than two years ago, said Bhutto's dismissal followed a growing list of complaints against her including a troubled economy.
He said he had known Pakistan's army chief General Jehangir Karamat during his tenure as Indian high commissioner (ambassador) in Islamabad.
"It seems that Farooq Leghari and Karamat will rule the roost," Dixit said.
He said Karamat did not appear to be an anti-India militarist. "He was not the sort of person who would try to seek a military solution to the problems with India," he said.
"The decision to dismiss Bhutto was probably taken after the intelligence agencies decided that the opposition campaign against her could not be contained without her removal," he added.
